title: The tree by the water (Psalm 1)
hook: the happy person is like a tree planted by rivers

segments.voice: Yesterday we closed the wilderness road, bemidbar, from slavery to the edge of the land. Your line was carried through the desert. What season of your own were you carried through? Day four hundred twelve, and a new block begins.

Today we open a different kind of book. Not a story this time. A songbook. A hundred and fifty poems: praise and complaint, thanks and rage, songs for a crowd and songs for one person awake at night. Monks chant them in the dark before dawn. People whisper them at bedsides. The Psalms. For the next fifty days, this path reads the Psalms and the wisdom books, a psalm a day to start. And the very first psalm, the front door to the whole collection, doesn't open with a command or a story. It opens with a picture. A tree, growing beside a stream.
screen: `A NEW BLOCK: THE PSALMS.` → `A HUNDRED AND FIFTY SONGS.` → `THE FRONT DOOR IS A TREE.`

segments.voice: Psalm one begins, in the King James Bible: "Blessed is the man that walketh not in the counsel of the ungodly, nor standeth in the way of sinners, nor sitteth in the seat of the scornful." Notice the slow drift. Walking. Then standing. Then sitting. First you're just passing by bad advice, then you stop and linger, then you've pulled up a chair and become a scoffer yourself. Nobody sits down all at once. Blessed here is the Hebrew ashrei, which also means happy, or how fortunate. The book of praises opens with: oh, the happiness of. Then: "But his delight is in the law of the LORD; and in his law doth he meditate day and night." Meditate, in Hebrew hagah, is a sound word. It's used elsewhere for a dove's moan and a lion's growl over its prey. To meditate on scripture was to murmur it under your breath, over and over, chewing on it. And then the picture: "And he shall be like a tree planted by the rivers of water, that bringeth forth his fruit in his season; his leaf also shall not wither." In a dry land, a tree beside an irrigation channel is a small miracle. Its roots go down to water nobody sees. It still has seasons. It doesn't fruit all year. But it doesn't dry up in the heat. The psalm ends with the other kind of life, which it calls chaff, the husks that blow away on the threshing floor. Two ways, the last verse says: the way of the righteous, and the way of the ungodly. Right at the door of the book. Saint Benedict's Rule for monks spreads all hundred and fifty psalms across each week, and some communities still keep that weekly round.
screen: `WALK, STAND, SIT: THE SLOW DRIFT.` · `ASHREI: OH, THE HAPPINESS.` · `HAGAH: MURMUR IT, LIKE A DOVE.` · `ROOTS DOWN TO HIDDEN WATER.` · then, large: `LIKE A TREE PLANTED BY THE RIVERS OF WATER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: sit by water or a tree. If you can, go to one now, or just to a window where you can see one. If you can't, picture one: a tree you know, beside a creek or a canal or a fountain. Settle, and breathe. Imagine its roots spreading underground, reaching down toward water you can't see. Then murmur one line under your breath, the old way, again and again: planted by the water. If you pray, you can ask where your roots are reaching. The bell holds the time.
Ashrei. Hebrew for blessed, happy, how fortunate, the first word of the Psalms: the life rooted like a tree by hidden water, fruit in its season.
Your line: planted by the water. Today, notice what you drift toward, walking, standing, sitting, and give five minutes to whatever waters your roots. Day four hundred twelve.

howItsDone: Christians pray the Psalms in the Liturgy of the Hours, in the Anglican Daily Office and in personal devotions; some monastic communities pray the whole Psalter each week.

what it means: a picture at the door of the Psalms: a life rooted in hidden water, with seasons, that doesn't wither in the heat.
what a scholar hears: ashrei, the Psalter's first word; hagah, murmuring meditation; and Benedict's Rule, praying all 150 psalms each week.

notes: Editor review (y2 days 407–424): hook cut the unsourced "gathered over centuries", "Jesus very likely knew by heart" and "fifteen hundred years", and the hospital image now used on days 416, 418 and 423; "Christians have prayed the Psalms from the beginning" and "many monks and nuns still pray them that way" replaced with what Benedict's Rule itself says; "two roads" (day 408) replaced with Psalm 1:6's two ways; practice drops the botanical claim about root spread; howItsDone rewritten.
Day 412 opens Block C (Psalms and wisdom books, days 412–461); review picks up day 411's carry from the index.
Hagah used of a lion growling (Isaiah 31:4) and of mourning like a dove (Isaiah 38:14; 59:11): standard lexicon. Confirm.
Hook now says monks chant the Psalms 'in the dark before dawn' (Benedict's Rule, night office/Vigils); confirm phrasing.
'Rivers of water' (palgei mayim) are channels, often irrigation; the script says 'irrigation channel'. Confirm.
Softened 'that Jesus would have known by heart' to 'very likely knew by heart': the Gospels show him quoting Psalms (e.g. 22, 110), but memorizing the whole Psalter is an inference. Confirm.
'Gathered over centuries' reflects mainstream scholarship; traditional attributions (many to David) differ. Confirm the phrasing is fair to both.
